prompt: A team selects an algorithm solely because its label is O(n log n), claiming that this proves a one-second deadline. Here n is item count and log is a base-two logarithm. What is missing?

options.text: Nothing: the label includes exact operation counts
options.explanation: Big-O hides coefficients and permits a loose bound.
Implementation, inputs and actual operations also affect performance.

options.text: A proof that every input is the best case
options.explanation: Best-case performance would not guarantee the workload deadline.

options.text: Input bounds, operation costs and representative measurements
options.explanation: Correct. A growth label alone cannot establish a finite elapsed-time budget.

workedExample: Identify the largest input and the operation being counted. Estimate work using an explicit model, then measure relevant implementations and data. Include allocation, output and memory effects where needed. The growth class is useful for screening candidates, not proving a one-second runtime.

prompt: A once-a-day job must find an exact subset among a tightly bounded small set of items. Checking each candidate is cheap. What is a sensible first approach?

options.text: Reject exhaustive search solely because it is exponential
options.explanation: Exponential scaling does not make every fixed small instance infeasible.

options.text: Enumerate all orderings even though only membership matters
options.explanation: Orderings repeat many representations of the same subset and solve a different search problem.

options.text: Prototype subset enumeration and check measured time against the budget
options.explanation: Correct. The bounded input and cheap checks may make the simplest exact method suitable.

options.text: Assume a heuristic must be used
options.explanation: A heuristic may miss a valid exact answer; infeasibility has not been established.

workedExample: Estimate candidates and per-candidate work under the actual maximum input. An exact exhaustive prototype can be simple and easy to validate. Benchmark it against the daily job budget and retain headroom. There is no universal item cutoff that settles every subset-search workload.

prompt: You estimate a large job’s runtime using iteration throughput measured on a representative small benchmark. Which finding most directly challenges that extrapolation?

options.text: The CPU clock frequency is larger than the measured iteration rate
options.explanation: An iteration can need many cycles; clock frequency is not iteration throughput.

options.text: The larger working set crosses a cache or memory boundary and slows each iteration
options.explanation: Correct. The assumed per-iteration rate may stop being representative at the larger size.

options.text: The benchmark was repeated to expose variation
options.explanation: Repeating measurements improves evidence rather than invalidating it.

options.text: The operation count is known exactly
options.explanation: An exact count helps; converting it to time still needs a representative rate.

workedExample: The estimate divides work by a rate. If the rate changes as the workload grows, the prediction must change too. Compare data layout, allocation and memory behaviour at representative large sizes, and report a range when throughput varies.
